lesson.title: Resonance: When the Inductor and Capacitor Fight to a Draw
lesson.summary: Resonance is the condition where inductive and capacitive reactance cancel exactly, leaving a series RLC circuit purely resistive with current at its maximum.
lesson.body:
Resonance in a series RLC circuit is the specific frequency at which the inductor's reactance and the capacitor's reactance are equal in magnitude but opposite in effect, so they cancel each other out completely, leaving the circuit's total impedance purely resistive. Inductive reactance, X_L equals omega L, grows with frequency, while capacitive reactance, X_C equals 1 over (omega C), shrinks with frequency. There is exactly one frequency where these two curves cross, and that crossing point is the resonant frequency omega_0, the same quantity used to build quality factor in the previous chapter.

At resonance, the circuit's impedance drops to its minimum possible value, Z equals R alone, since the reactive parts have cancelled. A minimum impedance in a series circuit means a maximum current for a given source voltage, and it also means the current and voltage are exactly in phase, since there is no reactance left to shift them. This is the defining physical signature of resonance: current peaks, phase angle goes to zero, and the circuit behaves for that one frequency as if the inductor and capacitor were not there at all, electrically speaking, even though energy is actively surging back and forth between them the entire time.

Work through the same circuit used throughout this unit: R equals 100 ohms, L equals 1 H, C equals 1 microfarad, resonant frequency omega_0 equals 1000 rad/s. At resonance, X_L equals omega_0 L equals 1000 times 1, which is 1000 ohms, and X_C equals 1 over (omega_0 C) equals 1 over (1000 times 0.000001), which is 1 over 0.001, also 1000 ohms. The two reactances match exactly, confirming resonance, and the total impedance is Z equals R equals 100 ohms.

Now drive this circuit with a 10 V rms source at resonance. The current is I equals V over Z equals 10 over 100, which is 0.1 A. The voltage across the inductor is V_L equals I times X_L equals 0.1 times 1000, which is 100 V, and the voltage across the capacitor is V_C equals I times X_C equals 0.1 times 1000, also 100 V. Both of these voltages are ten times larger than the 10 V source itself. This is not a mistake; it is voltage magnification, a hallmark of resonance in a series circuit with meaningful Q. In fact the ratio V_L over the source voltage equals 100 over 10, which is 10, exactly matching the quality factor Q equals 10 computed for this same circuit in the previous chapter. That is the physical meaning of Q made concrete: it is literally the factor by which the reactive voltages exceed the source voltage at resonance, even though those two large voltages are 180 degrees out of phase with each other and cancel when added, leaving the resistor to carry the full 10 V of the source alone.
